    Sell These Items While They’re Still Worth Money

    Cops Can Ticket You for This One Bad Driving Habit

    Somebody in your family kept a box. The masking tape label has gone soft, the flaps are still folded over each other, and nobody has opened it since roughly 1984. It is behind the Christmas decorations, and it is worth twenty minutes of your Saturday.

    Recommended for you

    The 1970s have become the decade collectors chase hardest, and the auction numbers are not subtle. A pair of handmade Nike Moon Shoes, designed by Nike co-founder Bill Bowerman for the 1972 Olympic Trials in a run of only about 12 pairs, sold at Sotheby’s in 2019 for $437,500. A 1973 Andy Warhol “Mao” painting brought $3.65 million. A WBC heavyweight belt awarded to Muhammad Ali after the Rumble in the Jungle, one of only two known to exist, sold at Heritage Auctions in 2022 for $6.18 million.

    You do not have a Warhol. What regular families do have, and what actually sells, comes down to five categories: original Kenner Star Wars toys, first pressing records, 1971 Topps baseball cards, early Atari and Apple hardware, and the plain household stuff (Pyrex, lunch boxes, lava lamps) that everybody used and almost everybody threw away.

    Original Kenner Star Wars Toys, Especially Still On The Card

    The ceiling here is absurd. A 1979 Kenner rocket-firing Boba Fett prototype sold for $1.3 million. It was built for a 1978 mail-away promotion in Kenner’s original “Star Wars” line, introducing a character who would not reach screens until 1980. Kenner scrapped the spring-loaded launcher after federal regulators recalled Mattel’s missile-firing Battlestar Galactica toys in January 1979 over a choking death, and only a handful of prototypes exist. That figure was never in a store, so it is not in your attic.

    Loose figures from the 1977 wave are a different story, and the prices are sane. A well-kept Luke has been listed on eBay around $250, and a set of a dozen originals including Luke, Leia and Darth Vader sold for $265. So the whole shoebox of scratched figures with missing blasters is lunch money plus a tank of gas, not a down payment.

    The money is in carded figures that were never opened, with the hanger hole at the top of the card still intact and unpunched. Earlier card backs are worth more than later ones, and small production variations matter more than the character does. If you find a sealed card, do not open it to “check” anything. Photograph both sides and leave it alone.

    Star Wars media rides the same wave. A sealed 1982 “drawer box” VHS of “Star Wars,” graded CGC 9.2 and one of about ten sealed copies known, sold for $23,750, which is an insane return on something that rented for a couple of bucks.

    First Pressing Records, Including The Ones Everybody Owned

    David Bowie’s “Diamond Dogs” is the poster child. RCA recalled the sleeve and airbrushed the genitals off Guy Peellaert’s dog illustration almost immediately after release, the earliest copies with the original artwork survived in small numbers, and one sold at auction for $16,250. On the regular resale market, first pressings with that art run around $3,500 and have reached $7,500.

    Common titles are worth checking too, which surprises people. Used, opened copies of The Eagles’ “Hotel California” and Fleetwood Mac’s “Rumours” are common enough that Discogs medians for 1977 first pressings sit near $20, but sealed first pressings of either are a different item and go for many times that. AC/DC’s first single, “Can I Sit Next to You, Girl,” released in Australia only in July 1974, is one of the decade’s most chased 45s, and the highest documented sale is about $4,500. Japanese pressings also carry a premium with serious collectors, which is why an album that looks identical to yours can be listed at ten times the price.

    Flip the record over before you get excited. The label text, the catalog number and the scratched-in codes in the smooth dead wax near the center are what separate a first pressing from a 1980s reissue worth about the same as a fast food combo. Store them standing upright, not stacked flat, and do not play the good ones. Every spin takes a little off the value.

    Paper from the same era sells as well. A 1970 Boston Tea Party concert poster showing Frank Zappa as the Mona Lisa sold for $10,313. If there are rolled-up show posters in the same closet, they are not scrap.

    1971 Topps Baseball Cards And Their Chipped Black Borders

    A 1971 Topps Johnny Bench graded PSA 9, one of only eight and the highest grade the card exists in, sold for $42,000. The set has black borders that chip if you look at them wrong, so clean, sharp-cornered examples barely exist, and that scarcity is doing most of the work on the price. Pull your 1971s out and look at the four edges under a lamp before you look at the player.

    Rookie cards from the decade are the other lottery ticket. A 1973 Topps rookie card sharing space between Ron Cey, John Hilton and Mike Schmidt has sold for $317,200 in PSA 10. Hockey counts too: a 1979-80 O-Pee-Chee Wayne Gretzky rookie graded PSA 10 sold at Goldin in 2016 for $465,000.

    Grading is the whole ballgame on cards. A PSA 10 can be worth 5 to 20 times the same card ungraded, which is why research firms put the sports card market somewhere above $12 billion in 2024. It also means submitting a stack of beat-up commons is just mailing money away. Send the two or three that look untouched, keep the rest in penny sleeves, and never try to clean, trim or flatten a card. Collectors spot it instantly and the card becomes worthless.

    Early Atari, Apple And Polaroid Hardware

    The Apple-1 is the one that changes a life. It sold for $666.66 in 1976, roughly 200 were built and about 175 of those actually sold, and the registry that tracks them counts around 80 survivors. One, professionally restored and signed by Steve Wozniak, sold on eBay for around $340,000 in 2022, and another brought $905,000 at Bonhams in 2014. It looks like a bare circuit board, not a computer, which is exactly why a few have turned up in garages.

    More likely, you have Atari. The 1977 VCS console, renamed the Atari 2600 in 1982, has been listed well over $600 in well-preserved shape. Games matter separately: a sealed first-production copy of Atari’s 1980 Space Invaders for the 2600, graded Wata 9.2, sold for $9,600. Check the cartridges before you dump the box at Goodwill.

    Two more from the same drawer. The first Sony Walkman, the TPS-L2, went on sale in Japan in July 1979 and reached America a year later badged the Soundabout, and a well-kept working one sold on eBay for $800. The Polaroid SX-70 hit the market in 1972 and working examples run from about $100 to well over $1,000 depending on condition, because people still shoot instant film.

    With electronics, working beats pretty. Put in fresh batteries, test it, and film a ten second video of it powering on. Then list every cord, manual, and the original foam packaging, because buyers pay for the complete kit and lowball anything described as “untested.”

    The Pyrex, Lunch Boxes And Lava Lamps Nobody Thought Twice About

    Pyrex is the sleeper, and sets beat singles every time. A set of four bowls in the classic Cinderella shape, the spouted and handled mixing bowls Corning made in dozens of patterns, sold on eBay for $125, and a set of four larger bowls in a bright dot pattern has been listed near $500. The chipped mixing bowl your mom still uses for pancake batter is probably worth more than the mixer.

    Metal lunch boxes with the matching thermos are next, and the character drives the number. A rare 1976 Disney set has been listed near $380, while a Charlie’s Angels box sits around $170. Vintage Lava Lite lamps in unusual colors or odd base shapes ask around $250, so the one in the basement rec room is not landfill.

    Boxed toys are where the household category gets loud. A 1976 Stretch Armstrong with the box and instructions has been listed at $2,800. “Talking Busy” Barbie has sold for well over $200 with her original box even when the talker is dead and the wear is obvious, and a Talking Busy Ken sold for more than $150. A loose 1978 Simon game is a $30 or $40 item, but unopened ones have sold for well over $100. That gap between opened and sealed repeats across every one of these categories.

    Two other odds and ends from the decade, for reference. A 1970 Donruss Odder Odd Rods wax box, the kind that held 24 packs of goofy hot rod trading cards, sold for $7,200 unopened. And a 1970 Batman #227 with the Neal Adams cover, a nod to Detective Comics #31 from 1939, sold for $19,200 in CGC 9.8, one of nine at that grade.

    Do This Before You List Anything

    Condition is the multiplier on all of it. Mint examples routinely bring ten times what a worn one does, and sometimes far more. That math means the single dumbest thing you can do is “tidy up” a find: no scrubbing, no touch-up paint, no new tape on an old box, no cutting a figure off its card.

    Ignore asking prices, including the ones above that say listed rather than sold. On eBay, filter to sold listings and look at the last 90 days. A lot of the eye-watering numbers floating around are people asking, not people getting paid, and the difference between a $2,800 ask and a $900 sale is your whole weekend.

    Get the stuff out of the attic today. Heat, damp and sunlight are what turn a $600 record into a $15 record. Clear plastic bins with latching lids from Walmart or Home Depot run about $10 to $15, and a hall closet is a better home than the garage rafters. Records go upright, cards go in sleeves, boxed toys go in a bin by themselves so nothing crushes a corner.

    Professional grading is worth the fee only on the top few pieces. It has spread far past cards, too: vintage Dungeons & Dragons books from the era now get graded and sealed in hard plastic slabs before they cross the auction block.

    My honest read after going through the numbers: cards and records are the easiest to actually turn into money, because the buyers are everywhere and the pricing is public. Sealed toys and boxed electronics pay the most per item but sell slowly, and you need patience to get the real number instead of the first offer. The household stuff (Pyrex, lunch boxes, lamps) is genuine money in the hundreds, just not the kind that makes a headline. Open the box anyway.
